open-question.question: This mission refuses a new Short Title holding a `/` at `add`, because the alternatives agent writes its return to a file named by the title. Most fixed calls also substitute the title inside a double-quoted shell argument, where `"`, `$`, a backtick, and `\` are special, and only the answer sweep's batched call states an escaping rule for it. Which further characters, if any, does `add` refuse in a new Short Title: none, those four, or everything outside an allow-list of letters, digits, spaces, and a fixed set of punctuation?
open-question.alternative: `add` refuses no character beyond the `/` the mission already refuses: `"`, `$`, backtick, `\`, and control characters are all accepted in a new Short Title, and every fixed call keeps substituting the title as an unescaped literal inside double quotes, the double-quoted positions recorded as an accepted gap. No title anyone writes is refused for a character that has never broken anything here: every id in this repository's history uses only letters, digits, spaces, `-`, and `.` (one escaping test fixture aside), and the tool, its help text, and the review pass's rule gain nothing beyond the slash check. A title holding `"`, `$`, a backtick, or `\` still breaks or silently changes the argument at every double-quoted call but the sweep's, a backtick running its text as a command, and a control character passes `add` and leaves `open_questions.xml` malformed so that every later tool call on the mission is refused (checked on 2026-11-25 with `\x01`); whether a `"` also breaks the recommendation pass's hand-rendered attributes depends on how that sibling question settles.

`add` refuses no character beyond `/`; instead the sweep's rule, that every title written inside double quotes has any `"`, `$`, backtick, or `\` escaped by a backslash, is stated at every other fixed call and procedure step that substitutes a Short Title (the review pass's `add` and `remove`, the recommendation pass's `embed`, `lift`, and `printf`, the answer core's `locate`, `remove`, and `lift`, the `strip` calls); control characters stay accepted. No title is ever refused, and the shell positions are closed where they break, in the same form the sweep already uses and its batched-call test already pins, so the set of characters a title may hold stays open. Correctness rests on every runner escaping correctly at a dozen sites, most of them in calls no fixed-call test extracts, which is the per-runner escaping the tools exist to remove; a control character still corrupts the document at `add`, and whether a `"` still breaks the hand-rendered attributes depends on how that sibling question settles.

`add` refuses, beside `/`, every control character (C0 and DEL) in the folded title, the one class that makes the tool itself write a malformed document; `"`, `$`, backtick, and `\` stay accepted and the double-quoted positions stay as they are, recorded as an accepted gap. It closes the one failure that damages state rather than one call, a title that leaves `open_questions.xml` unreadable to every later tool call, at the cost of refusing nothing a person would write, so no recorded or plausible title is affected. The four double-quote characters keep breaking or silently changing every fixed call but the sweep's, a backtick running as a command, and whether a `"` breaks the hand-rendered attributes depends on how that sibling question settles.

`add` refuses, beside `/`, every control character (C0 and DEL); the four double-quote characters stay accepted and the sweep's backslash-escaping rule is stated at every other fixed call and procedure step that substitutes a Short Title. The document can no longer be corrupted by a title, and the shell positions are closed without refusing any printable character, so a title may still hold a quote, a dollar sign, or a backslash. The shell positions still rest on every runner escaping correctly at a dozen sites, most of them untested, and the rule must be written into each of them; whether a `"` still breaks the hand-rendered attributes depends on how that sibling question settles.

`add` refuses, beside `/`, the four characters special inside double quotes, `"`, `$`, backtick, and `\`, in the folded title, a deny-list of five; control characters stay accepted and the fixed calls stay as shown, with no escaping rule needed for a new title. It closes both named uses of the title, the file name and the double-quoted argument, with one check of the same shape as the slash refusal, refusing characters no recorded title has ever held, so every call site stays exactly as shown. A control character still passes `add` and leaves the document unreadable to every later call, and the deny-list names only the failures found so far, so a position found later needs another addition; blocks authored before it keep their titles, a case a sibling question owns.

`add` refuses, beside `/`, the four double-quote characters `"`, `$`, backtick, and `\` and every control character (C0 and DEL) in the folded title; the fixed calls stay as shown, with no escaping rule needed for a new title. Every failure known for a Short Title is closed at its one creation point, the file name, the double-quoted argument, and the malformed document, while every printable character outside the four stays allowed, so no title a person would plausibly write is refused. It is still a deny-list of the failures found so far, so a later-found position needs another addition, and the refusal message and the review pass's rule must name a longer set; blocks authored before it keep their titles, a case a sibling question owns.

`add` refuses every character of the folded title outside an allow-list: letters and digits as Unicode classes them, the space, and a fixed set of punctuation (for instance `-`, `_`, `.`, `,`, `'`, `(`, `)`, `:`, `?`), which leaves out `/`, the four double-quote characters, control characters, and any other symbol; the fixed calls stay as shown. It closes the whole class rather than the failures found so far, so a position discovered later cannot break on a character a title may hold, and every recorded title, which uses only letters, digits, spaces, `-`, and `.`, still passes. It refuses characters no one has shown to break anything (an em dash, `&`, `+`, `#`), the punctuation set is one more fixed list the tool and the review pass's rule must state, and whether `.` and a leading `-` belong in it depends on how the separator and leading-dash sibling questions settle.

open-question.question: Once `add` refuses certain characters in a new Short Title, where is the rule stated: only in the open-question tool's help text and `Error:` line, with the review pass's Short Title rule naming the refusal as it names the duplicate-id refusal, or also as a statement in that rule of what a Short Title may hold, so the author writes a valid title the first time?
open-question.alternative: The refusal is stated only by the open-question tool: its module docstring and `add` help text name the refused characters, and its `Error:` line names the one a refused title holds. The Short Title bullet in `review-mission-requirements` is left as it stands, naming only the duplicate-id refusal, and no other runtime file mentions the character rule. The character set has one home, the tool that enforces it, so no prose copy can drift from it when the set changes. It also fits the rule that runtime prose states a tool's contract in at most one sentence per site. The cost is low: none of the 478 recorded block ids holds `/`, `"`, `$`, a backtick, or `\`, a refused `add` leaves the document byte-identical, and the author only retries with the `Error:` line in hand. The author learns the rule only from a refusal. The draft's trigger, `tools/README.md headroom`, shows that a path-like title comes naturally when a question concerns one file, so each such title costs the review pass an extra turn. The bullet also stays silent about a refusal that sits right beside the duplicate-id one it already names.

The tool's help text and `Error:` line state the rule as in the tool-only form. The review pass's Short Title bullet gains one clause naming the refusal the way it names the duplicate-id refusal: the tool refuses a title holding a character it cannot carry, its `Error:` line names it, and the author picks another title and calls again. The clause lists no characters. The bullet now tells the author that a character refusal exists and how to recover, in the same shape as the duplicate-id clause. The character set stays in the tool alone, so whatever set the refusal ends up holding needs no prose change. Without the characters, the author still cannot avoid them up front, so the first path-like or quoted title is still refused and retried. The clause mostly repeats what the `Error:` line already says when it fires.

The tool's help text and `Error:` line state the rule. The review pass's Short Title bullet gains one clause naming the refusal and listing the characters `add` refuses, framed as a refusal: the tool refuses a title holding any of them, its `Error:` line names the one found, and the author picks another title. The author can avoid every refused character before the first call, so a valid title is written the first time. The clause also keeps the shape the bullet already uses for the duplicate-id refusal, a statement of what the tool refuses rather than a new authoring rule. The character set now has two homes, the tool and the review pass's prose, and they must change together or the prose will name a set the tool no longer enforces. How long the clause is depends on how many characters the sibling question on refused characters settles: a short list for `/` or the four shell-active characters, an unwieldy one if the set is defined by an allow-list.

The tool's help text and `Error:` line state the rule. The review pass's Short Title bullet also gains a positive statement of what a Short Title may hold, as an authoring rule: plain words of the characters the tool accepts, with a file or path the question concerns named by its role in the title and written out in the question text. The tool's refusal is named after that statement as the backstop, with the author picking another title on its `Error:` line. It meets the question's aim of a valid title on the first attempt most directly. It tells the author not only which characters to avoid but how to phrase a title about one file, which is the case that triggered the draft. A rule stated in terms of what is allowed also reads naturally if the accepted set is an allow-list. It adds an authoring rule beside the bullet's existing ones and a second statement of the character set, which must track the tool's set exactly. Rules on phrasing are judgment that no test pins. How well it fits depends on the sibling questions on refused characters and on the answer-text separator: for example, whether a `.`, and with it every file name, is ruled out of a title.

open-question.question: The refusal of characters in a Short Title runs only at `add`, so a block authored before it keeps its title, and a title holding a `/` fails the alternatives agent's file write on every run, leaving the block without alternatives. What happens to an existing block whose Short Title a new `add` would refuse: is it left as it stands, to be re-authored by hand, or does the review pass re-author it under a valid title as cleanup?
open-question.alternative: No runner acts on an existing block whose Short Title a new `add` would refuse: `load_document` keeps validating ids for duplicates only, the review pass gains no rule for such a block, and the alternatives pass dispatches it as it does any bare block. The alternatives agent's path-separator clause stays, reworded as the case of a block authored before the refusal, so a `/` title keeps ending in a `FAILED:` whose reason names the separator in each run's advisory. Re-authoring is left to the operator, who runs the open-question tool's existing `remove` and `add` with a valid title, the document never edited by hand. Changes nothing beyond the clause rewording, and it matches the draft's settled reasoning that only `add` checks and the plugin-wide stance that no migration ships for forms an earlier copy left behind; no live document in this repository holds such a title, and the draft records that history has never needed a re-authoring. A `/` block is still dispatched and fails on every alternatives run, costing one agent each time, and the only sign of why is a `FAILED:` reason in an advisory; nothing tells the operator the remedy, and a block refused for another character keeps whatever shell-quoting breakage it carried, the size of that set depending on which characters the sibling question on refused characters settles on.

The block is left as it stands and nothing re-authors it, but the alternatives pass checks each gathered Short Title against the characters `add` refuses before dispatching, sends no agent for one that fails the check, and names it in its advisory under a fixed reason carrying the remedy (re-author it through the review pass or the tool's `remove` and `add`). The agent's path-separator clause stays as a backstop. Stops the repeated wasted dispatch and replaces an opaque `FAILED:` with a reason and remedy the operator can act on, while still re-authoring nothing and leaving the question text and every other block untouched. The refused set is stated a second time, in the orchestrator's prose, where a runner judges characters by reading ids instead of a tested tool doing it, and it can drift from `add`'s check; it adds an advisory reason to the pass and still leaves the fix to the operator, for a case no document in this repository has.

alternative.id: Review re-authors by remove and add

open-question.alternative: The review pass gains a third cleanup beside prune and dedup: for every block whose Short Title a new `add` would refuse, it runs the existing bare `remove` and then `add` under a new valid 2–5 word title with the question text carried verbatim, riding in the pass's `Requirements-review:` commit and recording nothing under `## Decisions`. The tool is unchanged; the block comes back bare, and `remove`'s cascade strips the pick of every block whose `<depends-on>` tag named it, keeping their alternatives. Closes the case automatically on the next review pass with tools the pass already calls, so a `/` block stops failing every alternatives run without the operator knowing the rule, and the fix lands where block ids are authored. Widens the review pass's removal rule beyond cleanup of recorded state, which the tidy-versus-record invariant limits to a covering decision or an exact duplicate; a block refused for a character other than `/` may already carry alternatives and a pick, which are lost with any dependents' picks and cost an alternatives and a recommendation re-run; how many blocks it reaches depends on the refused set the sibling question on refused characters settles.

The open-question tool gains a `rename` subcommand that changes one block's id to a new title, refusing it as `add` would refuse it, keeping every child of the block, and rewriting every `question` attribute of a `<depends-on>` tag naming the old id in the same write; the review pass calls it as cleanup for every block whose Short Title a new `add` would refuse, in its `Requirements-review:` commit. Re-authors the title with nothing lost: the block's alternatives and pick and every dependent's pick and tag survive, so no cascade strip and no annotation re-run follow, and the check reuses `add`'s own refusal. A new subcommand with its contract, help text, tests, and three rebuilt host copies, and a third tidy action in the review pass widening its cleanup beyond recorded state, all for a case this repository's history has never produced and that the no-migration stance would otherwise leave to the operator; its reach depends on the refused set the sibling question on refused characters settles.

open-question.question: A task's `##` heading is substituted into double-quoted shell arguments (`--subject "Task-completion: <TASK_NAME>"` in both completion calls, the title arguments of `submit-task` and of the task-list tool's `remove`), where `"`, `$`, a backtick, and `\` are special; only `submit-task` states an escaping rule, and this repository's recorded headings already hold a double quote. Does the task-list tool refuse those characters in a new task title, as `add` refuses characters in a Short Title, or are task titles handled another way or left as they are?
open-question.alternative: The task-list tool refuses a new title holding `"`, `$`, a backtick, or `\` at both points where a title is created, `insert` (submit-task) and `initialize` (derive-tasks, whose titles arrive inside the heredoc), with one `Error:` line naming the character and the file left unchanged; the help text states the refused set. The completion calls, the procedure's `remove`, and the orchestrator's `--subject` stay as shown, with no escaping rule added; submit-task keeps its existing rule for the anchors it names. Sections already standing in a list keep their headings. One check at the only two creation points makes every later substitution of the title into a double-quoted argument safe by construction, so the four completion-side sites need no rule a runner could misapply; of the 752 headings in this repository's task-list history only two hold any of the four characters (a `"` each), so almost nothing ordinary is refused. A heading created before the check, or written by a hand edit of the list (a condition on how queued-task revision is settled), still reaches the unescaped completion sites, where a `"` ends the quote and splits the title into several arguments; whether the refused set matches what `add` refuses for a Short Title depends on how that sibling settles.

As in refusing the four characters at `insert` and `initialize`, and in addition every site that substitutes a task title into a double-quoted shell argument (the completion procedure's `remove`, the inline `complete-task` call's `remove` and `--subject`, the agent's step-5 `remove`, and the orchestrator's commit-from-file `--subject`) states the escaping rule submit-task already states: `"`, `$`, a backtick, or `\` escaped by a backslash. New titles can never hold the characters, and a heading that predates the check or entered by hand still completes and commits correctly, so no queued list in any project is left with a task that cannot be removed. Two mechanisms for one failure: the rule's text is added to four sites and their rendered copies, and for every title created after the check it guards nothing, while correctness for the older headings still rests on each runner's escaping.

The task-list tool accepts a new title at `insert` and `initialize` only when every character is a letter, a digit, a space, or one of a fixed set of punctuation marks, refusing any other with one `Error:` line; the completion sites stay as shown with no escaping rule, and standing headings keep their text. Closes the shell-active class wholesale rather than by naming four characters, so a character no one has yet found special in some position (a `!`, a glob character, a control or non-ASCII byte) never reaches a command line either. Refuses ordinary titles the four-character set would accept, such as one holding an arrow, an accented letter, or punctuation left off the list, and the set has to be chosen and documented; like any creation-time check it leaves pre-existing and hand-written headings uncovered, and its fit with `add` depends on how the Short Title character question settles.

No title is refused. Every site that substitutes a task title into a double-quoted shell argument (the completion procedure's `remove`, the inline `complete-task` call, the agent's step-5 call, and the orchestrator's `--subject`) states the rule submit-task already states, `"`, `$`, a backtick, or `\` escaped by a backslash, and the fixed-call tests fill a title holding those characters through a helper applying that rule, as the sweep's batched-call test does for headings. No tool changes and no title is ever refused, so a heading holding a `"`, as two recorded ones do, stays writable; the rule is the one form already used at submit-task and the sweep, so every title-substituting site reads alike. Correctness stays in each runner's hands at four more sites, the completion agent being the population most given to rewriting commands, and a missed backtick runs its text as a command and still exits 0; the test pins the rule's application by a helper, not the runner's.

No title is refused and no tool changes. Each fixed call that substitutes a task title captures it once from a quoted heredoc in the group-fed form the completion calls already use for the bar (`{ title="$(cat)"; } <<'EOF'`) and passes `"$title"` to `remove` and `"Task-completion: $title"` to `--subject`: the inline `complete-task` call, the agent's step-5 call, the orchestrator's commit-from-file call, and submit-task's `insert` call for its new title and anchor; the procedure's bare `remove` is shown in the same form. The title is never shell-parsed, so every character, a `"` or a backtick included, reaches the tools verbatim with nothing for the runner to escape and nothing refused; it reuses a capture form already proven on bash 3.2 and pinned by the fixed-call tests. Every affected fence gains a second heredoc and a held variable, lengthening calls the runners already copy, and submit-task's escaping rule is replaced rather than extended; the heredoc's own terminator line is a new place a title could collide, which is the heredoc-delimiter sibling's concern.

No title is refused. The tools take the title outside the argument list: the task-list tool's `remove` (and `insert`'s title and anchors) read it from standard input or a named file, and the commit tool gains a form taking its subject from a file or standard input, so the completion calls and the orchestrator pass the title through a heredoc or a file the agent writes beside `paths.txt` and `body.txt`. Moves the guarantee into tested tools, so no runner's quoting is involved and the title reaches each tool byte for byte, whatever it holds. Reverses two recorded contracts, `remove` reading no stdin and the commit tool gaining no input forms beyond its arguments, adds a third agent file to the return contract, and changes every completion fence and its tests for a case two recorded headings have ever hit.

No title is refused and no site changes: submit-task keeps its escaping rule, the completion sites keep the bare double-quoted title, and CLAUDE.md records the case as accepted with its reason, that a `"`, `$`, backtick, or `\` in a task heading is rare (two of 752 recorded headings, both a `"`) and a failed `remove` stops the call before any commit. Costs nothing in tools, fences, or tests, and a failure surfaces as a refused or mis-split `remove` before the commit lands, so it does not record a wrong task silently. A backtick or `$` in a heading is expanded by the shell rather than refused, so the subject or the removal can silently carry the wrong text, and each runner keeps improvising its own quoting at the completion sites, the inconsistency the mission exists to close.

open-question.question: The commit procedure shows a commit body as the double-quoted literal `--body "<BODY>"`, where a backtick or `$` expands and a `"` ends the argument, and the skills following it pass Markdown text there (the finish summary, a hand answer's rationale, a lifted line); many recorded bodies hold such characters, so each runner has been changing the quoting on its own. How does a body reach the commit tool from the commit procedure: captured from a quoted heredoc and passed as a quoted variable, as the completion calls do, read by the tool from standard input or a file, or written as a literal under a stated escaping rule?
open-question.alternative: The commit procedure's shown command changes to the form the completion calls already use: the body is captured once from a quoted heredoc in the group-fed form `{ body="$(cat)"; } <<'EOF'`, under the clause telling the runner to pick a delimiter line the text does not contain, and passed on as `--body "$body"` in the same shell call, a BODY-less caller leaving both the capture and `--body` out as it leaves out `--body` now. The commit tool and its contract stay unchanged, every caller following the procedure by reference (`finish-mission`, `answer-open-question`, the two lift-based answer skills, `capture-mission-principle-updates`) gets the form through the procedure with no edit of its own, the fixed calls that already pass a captured value keep their calls, and the new command is pinned by a test extracting it from the rendered tree and running it on a body holding a backtick, a `$`, a `"`, and an apostrophe. It closes the expansion with no tool change and no revised invariant: the form is the one the shell-commands invariant already scopes as a single quoted value outside the variable ban and the one both completion calls run, so the plugin ends with one body-passing shape and the runner types the Markdown verbatim with nothing to escape. The text still passes through the shell, so it rests on the delimiter clause (a body line equal to the delimiter ends the heredoc and runs the rest as commands) and on the runner keeping the group-fed form, since the nested `$(cat <<'EOF'` form fails on bash 3.2 when the body holds an apostrophe; command substitution also drops the body's trailing newlines, harmless for git but a silent normalization.

The commit tool gains a standard-input body form (a flag such as `--body-stdin`, or `--body -`), and the commit procedure's command feeds BODY to it directly as a quoted heredoc, under the delimiter clause, with no shell variable in between; `--body` stays for the fixed calls that already pass a captured value (`$bar`, `$pick`, `$body`, the orchestrator's `$(cat "<scratch dir>/body.txt")`), which are left as they are. The tool's help text, its tests, and the committing invariant's statement that the tool gained no body option of its own are revised, and the procedure's command is pinned by an extracting test. It puts the commit tool on the plugin-wide convention every document writer already follows (free text on stdin as a quoted heredoc), so the body never becomes a shell value at all and the procedure's command keeps one process with nothing captured or re-passed. It changes a tool's contract and revises a recorded invariant for a failure a no-tool-change form also closes, leaves the tool with two body inputs whose precedence must be defined and tested, and still rests on the heredoc delimiter clause.

The commit tool takes its body from standard input only, `--body` retired: the commit procedure feeds BODY as a quoted heredoc under the delimiter clause, and every fixed call that passes a body today is rewritten to feed it the same way (both completion calls their heredoc straight to the tool, the orchestrator `< "<scratch dir>/body.txt"`, the sweep and the recommendation pass their held value through `printf '%s'`), with the tool's tests, the four fixed-call tests, and the committing invariant revised to match. One body input across the whole plugin, with no captured bar or held body re-passed through a quoted argument anywhere, so there is no second form for a runner to reach for and no precedence rule to define. It rewrites five working, tested fixed calls and their tests to fix the one site that is not fixed, and the completion calls' capture exists to test the bar for a non-blank line before `remove`, so they would still need the value in hand and the rewrite gains them nothing.

The commit tool gains a `--body-file FILE` option, and the commit procedure has the runner write BODY with its file-writing tool to a file outside the repository (a path made with `mktemp`, held as a path and written out in full, never kept in a shell variable) and then name it on the command line, the shell never touching the text; the orchestrator's `--body "$(cat …)"` may move onto the same option, the other fixed calls keeping `--body`. The tool's help text and tests, the committing invariant's no-body-file clause, and the procedure's command are revised and pinned by tests. It is the only form in which no shell parses the body at all, so no backtick, `$`, quote, apostrophe, or delimiter-looking line can affect it, and it extends the line-exact file read the tool already does for `--path-file`. It costs every committing caller an extra write turn and a temporary location (and since the plugin deletes no scratch file, a leftover body file per commit), and it reverses the committing invariant's explicit decision that the tool gained no body-file option.

The command stays the double-quoted literal `--body "<BODY>"`, and the commit procedure gains the escaping rule the answer sweep and `submit-task` already state for titles: every `"`, `$`, backtick, and `\` in BODY is escaped by a backslash; no tool changes, and a test fills the procedure's command through a helper applying the rule. It is the smallest edit, one sentence in one procedure, and it makes the body follow the same escaping rule the plugin already states for titles and headings, so a runner meets one quoting rule everywhere a literal is substituted. Correctness rests on every runner escaping every character of a Markdown body, and finish summaries and lifted lines are dense with backticks; one missed backtick runs its text as a command and the commit still lands with a mangled body and exit 0, the failure the question exists to close.

The command writes BODY as a single-quoted literal, `--body '<BODY>'`, and the commit procedure states its one escaping rule: every `'` in BODY is written as `'\''`; nothing else is special, no tool changes, and a test fills the command through a helper applying the rule. Only one character needs escaping instead of four, so backticks and `$`, the characters Markdown bodies hold most, pass through untouched with no tool change. Apostrophes are common in English prose and summaries, the `'\''` form is easy to get wrong and hard to read, a missed one still breaks the argument or runs text as shell, and it is a second quoting rule beside the double-quote rule the plugin states for titles.

Nothing changes: the commit procedure keeps the double-quoted literal with no rule, each runner keeps choosing its own quoting as it has been, and CLAUDE.md records the case as accepted with its reason. No edit to the procedure, the tool, or any test, and the field runs show runners already adapting the quoting themselves, so the commits that land mostly carry their bodies intact. The shown command stays wrong for the text it is given, so every runner that copies it literally expands a backtick or `$` or cuts the argument at a `"`, silently and with exit 0, and the run-to-run variation in quoting is exactly the unreproducible behaviour the mission sets out to close.

open-question.question: The answer sweep passes a decision's `###` heading to the fold tool as the double-quoted literal `--section "<Heading>"`, under its rule that `"`, `$`, a backtick, and `\` are escaped by a backslash; an unescaped backticked heading runs its text as a command, exits 0, and creates a mangled subsection, so correctness rests on each runner's escaping. Does the heading keep reaching the tool as an escaped literal, or does it reach it another way: a value captured from a quoted heredoc, standard input, or a file?
open-question.alternative: The heading keeps reaching `fold` and `replace` as the double-quoted literal `--section "<Heading>"` in the sweep's question and conflict sections, under the escaping rule the sweep already states (`"`, `$`, a backtick, and `\` escaped by a backslash); no fence, tool, or test changes, and CLAUDE.md records the exposure as accepted, with its reason, as the entry's outcome. Nothing changes and nothing new can break: the rule is already stated at the one site, the existing batched-call test already fills a heading holding characters the quotes must escape, and the field record shows no call ever ran with a raw backtick (12 of the 15 risky headings in 1,076 calls were escaped by the runner as told). Correctness keeps resting on each runner's escaping inside a call it is told to run exactly as shown; one missed backtick runs its text as a command, exits 0, and creates a mangled subsection that `fold` never refuses, and a backticked text naming a real command would run it.

The heading stays a literal on the command line but is written inside single quotes, `--section '<Heading>'`, in both sweep sections, the escaping rule narrowed for that position to one character: a `'` in the heading written as `'\''`; the tool and its contract are unchanged, and the batched-call test's helper fills the heading under the new rule. Inside single quotes `$`, backticks, `"`, and `\` are inert, so the failure the question names (a backticked heading run as a command) can no longer happen through any character but one, with no tool change and the call still one fixed fence. It is still a runner-applied escaping rule, now for the apostrophe, which recorded headings hold often (the tested failing heading itself, `The readers' `tasks` calls`, holds one); a missed `'` closes the quote early and leaves the rest of the heading, backticks included, unquoted, and the position then differs from the double-quoted form every other title, option, and subject in the same call uses.

Each sweep section captures its heading once from a quoted heredoc in the group-fed form the completion calls use for the bar (`{ heading="$(cat)"; } <<'EOF'`, the heading on the one line inside) and passes it on as `--section "$heading"` to `fold` or `replace`; the runner escapes nothing in the heading, the delimiter clause covers the new heredoc, the fold tool and its contract are unchanged, and the batched-call test fills a raw backticked heading through the new form. open-question.question: After a task removes a file with `git rm` or renames one with `git mv`, the commit tool's `git add` of the old path fails because the index no longer holds it, and the task's commit is refused; a file removed with a plain `rm` commits, and the completion procedure says nothing of how a task deletes or renames a file. How does a removed or renamed path get committed: does the commit tool stage only the paths the working tree or the index still holds and let its pathspec commit record the staged removal, or are runners told to remove and rename with plain commands?

The commit tool repeats every git write that exits 128, up to 16 attempts over about four seconds, reading only the exit status and never git's message, so a failure no lock caused, such as a pathspec matching no file, is repeated to the last attempt before its error prints. Does the tool keep repeating every exit 128, or does it stop at once on one no lock caused, which needs it to read git's message text or to tell the two cases apart some other way?
open-question.alternative: The commit tool keeps repeating every git write that exits 128 on the present schedule (16 attempts, 0.25 seconds apart), reading only the exit status and no message text. A failure no lock caused, such as `git add` of a pathspec matching no file, is still repeated to the last attempt before its `Error:` line prints. The committing invariant stays as written, and CLAUDE.md records the entry as accepted with its reason. Nothing changes in the tool, its tests, or the committing invariant, and no lock is ever missed because of git's wording, its locale, or a new lock message: the only cost is about four seconds before a failure that ends the call anyway, and git's own message still reaches the runner whole. Every non-lock 128 costs about four seconds and reports itself as "on all 16 attempts", which reads as a held lock and can send a runner to look for one; how often this happens depends on how the sibling question on committing a removed path settles, since that case is the one reproduced.

The tool keeps repeating every exit 128 without reading any message, but its one schedule constant is cut to a smaller window (for example a handful of attempts over about one second), so a non-lock failure surfaces sooner; nothing tells the two kinds of failure apart. The change is two constants and the retry test's bounds, with no message parsing and no new branch, and it shrinks the wasted wait on every non-lock failure in proportion. It narrows the window that absorbs another run's ordinary write, the reason the retry exists, below the bounds `tests/test_commit_retry.py` pins as decided, so concurrent runs (two completion runs, a sweep beside a completion run) collide more often; and a non-lock failure is still repeated and still reported as a multi-attempt failure.

After a write exits 128, the tool reads git's stderr and repeats the write only when it holds git's lock-file text (the `Unable to create '….lock': File exists` form that a held index, `HEAD`, or ref lock prints); every other exit 128 is passed on at once as one `Error:` line after its single attempt. Git is run with a fixed C locale so the message is not translated. The committing invariant's "no message text is read" is revised and the retry tests gain a non-lock 128 that fails on the first attempt. It stops exactly the failures that are not locks, whatever their cause, so a pathspec, repository, or permission failure is reported at once and honestly as one attempt, while every lock git reports in its standard form is still absorbed. The tool depends on git's message wording: a git version that rewords the lock message, or a lock failure printed in another form, is no longer retried and collides at once, the failure the retry was built to prevent; the fixed locale must cover every git write the tool runs.

After a write exits 128, the tool reads git's stderr and stops at once only when it matches a short stated list of failures no lock causes (starting with `pathspec '…' did not match any files`); every other exit 128, an unrecognized message included, is repeated on the present schedule. Git runs under a fixed C locale; the committing invariant is revised to name the list. A wording change in git or an unlisted message falls back to today's behaviour, so no lock is ever left unretried; the reproduced case and any later one found in the field stop at once. It closes only the failures someone has listed, so each new non-lock 128 still waits the full window until it is added, and the list is message-matching code the tool must keep current with git; if the sibling question on removed paths stops the pathspec case from reaching git, the list may hold nothing that occurs.

After a write exits 128, the tool reads no message text but checks git's own lock files, resolved through `git rev-parse --git-path` (the index lock, `HEAD.lock`, and the current branch's ref lock): it repeats the write while one of them exists, repeats it once more when none exists so a lock released between the failure and the probe is still absorbed, and passes on a further 128 with no lock file present after that second attempt. It tells a lock from a non-lock by the lock itself rather than by git's wording or locale, so the invariant's "no message text is read" can stand, and a non-lock failure ends after two attempts instead of sixteen. The tool gains file probes and a branch on what git keeps under its directory, a lock it does not probe (another ref, a packed-refs or config lock) is treated as a non-lock after two attempts, and the retry test must hold each probed lock file, so the mechanics grow more than a message match would.

Is this closed, by a rule in the agent's file or a step in the orchestrator, or only recorded as accepted?

The `complete-task` agent's file rules out any payload above its bare `DONE`, yet since 2026-11-18 58 of 415 `DONE` returns carried a summary above the token; the orchestrator reads the last line only, so the cost is the text it has to hold. Is this closed by a change to the agent's file, or only recorded as accepted?
open-question.alternative: Change the `complete-task` agent's file, in its `## Return protocol` section only. The return changes from "exactly one of these as the final line" to a final message that is exactly the one line and nothing else, `DONE` or `FAILED: <reason>`, matching how the alternatives agent's file words its own return ("the bare token `DONE` as your final message and nothing else", with any remaining thinking done in an earlier turn). No sentence is added at step 5. `complete-all-tasks` keeps reading the last line only, so its verdict and its no-status stop stay as they are. CLAUDE.md records the entry as fixed by this rewording. No tool and no fixed call changes, so no test is added. It removes the wording most likely to invite the summary: "final line" allows text above the token, and "the whole message" does not. It also gives the plugin's two dispatched agents one return form, written once in each file's return section. It is a prose-only change with nothing that checks it. Whether the 58 of 415 rate drops can only be seen in later field runs, and the rule stays in the return section, which the agent reads before it starts the task, far from the moment it writes `DONE`. Where the sibling question on returns without a token also rewrites this section, the two edits must be worded together.

Leave the `## Return protocol` wording as it stands ("final line", no payload above it). Add one sentence directly after the agent's step-5 call: once that call succeeds, the agent's next and last message is the bare `DONE`, with no summary of the work, the files, or the bar. The orchestrator stays unchanged. CLAUDE.md records the entry as fixed by this sentence. No tool and no fixed call changes, so no test is added. It puts the rule at the point where the summary is written, the turn right after the last call succeeds, rather than only in a section the agent read before any work began. It also leaves the contract's existing wording, and the invariant that quotes it, untouched. The contract keeps saying "final line", which still technically allows text above the token. The rule ends up stated in two places in one file, the sort of restatement the files otherwise avoid. Like any prose change, its effect can only be measured in later field runs.

Do both. Reword the `## Return protocol` so the final message is exactly the one token line and nothing else, as the alternatives agent's file words it, and add the one sentence after the step-5 call making the next and last message the bare `DONE`. The orchestrator keeps its last-line read. CLAUDE.md records the entry as fixed by the two edits. No tool and no fixed call changes, so no test is added. It is the strongest change the agent's file can make. The contract no longer allows text above the token, and the rule appears again at the exact turn where the summary was being written. It is the largest prose change to a contract that already works, because the orchestrator's last-line read is unaffected by the summary, and it states the rule twice in one file. It is still unenforced, and whether it works can only be judged from later field runs.

Drop the ban instead of enforcing it. The agent's `## Return protocol` allows a short summary above the final `DONE` line and states that the orchestrator ignores it, `complete-all-tasks` keeps reading the last line only, and the return-contracts invariant in CLAUDE.md is revised to say a summary above the token is allowed and unread. The file then matches what agents already do, so no rule is left that 14% of returns break, and nothing needs enforcing or measuring. It reverses a recorded invariant, and it invites text in all 415 returns rather than 58. That grows exactly the cost the question names: text the orchestrator holds for every task of an unattended run but never reads. It also leaves the two dispatched agents with different return forms.

Change neither the agent's file nor the orchestrator. CLAUDE.md records this entry's outcome as accepted, permanently: the count (58 of 415 `DONE` returns since 2026-11-18) and the reason, which is that the orchestrator's verdict reads the last line only and so is never affected, and the cost is bounded to the summary text it holds per task. It costs nothing and risks nothing. The verdict is already robust to the summary, and no prose change is made whose effect cannot be checked inside this mission. The agent's file goes on stating a rule that about one return in seven breaks, a contract and a behaviour knowingly left apart. The orchestrator keeps paying the held text on every such task, which adds up over a long `complete-all-tasks` run.
